title: Fake ICE Agents Are Targeting Northeastern Students, Campus Police Chief Says
dek: Northeastern University's police chief told student leaders his department is investigating numerous cases of people impersonating immigration agents on campus, and that his officers cannot keep the real ones out.
body: At Northeastern University, the immigration agents students fear most may not be immigration agents at all.

Ruben Galindo, chief of the Northeastern University Police Department, told the school's Student Government Association on Oct. 5 that his officers are investigating numerous cases of people posing as agents of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on campus, according to The Huntington News, the university's independent student newspaper. Universal Hub highlighted the report on Oct. 19.
Galindo described scams aimed at students as one of the department's main challenges.
> "The real threat that exists here." — Ruben Galindo, Northeastern University police chief
Neither the student paper nor Universal Hub reported how the impersonators approach students, what they demand, or whether anyone has lost money. The chief did not give a number of cases.
## A Campus on Edge

The warning lands on a campus where fear of immigration enforcement has become a constant presence. The Huntington News reported that the topic became a flashpoint after the Trump administration's revocations of student visas.

In the most recent student government election, Northeastern students overwhelmingly approved a referendum calling for stronger immigration protections and for students to be informed of their rights in encounters with ICE, the paper reported. The referendum says concerns about ICE violating students' rights on campus have increased, and that many students of color do not feel protected or safe on university property.

It asks the university to publish a clear statement of students' rights and to train administrators and staff on how to respond if ICE officers appear. Galindo told student leaders he was not familiar with the referendum and would look into it, according to the paper.
## Who Gets Through the Door

Galindo said he is not worried about ICE coming to campus, the Huntington News reported. He pointed to the fact that international students, faculty and researchers must hold valid visas to be at Northeastern.

If agents do show up, he said, his first step is to confirm they actually work for the agency, and his second is to confirm their authority to be there. But he acknowledged that NUPD has no power to stop other law enforcement agencies, ICE included, from entering campus.

ICE officers have visited the campus before for what Galindo called administrative investigations, and they notified campus police ahead of time, he said. In a follow-up email to the paper, he described ICE inspections as random and routine.
The Huntington News reported that the university did not answer its question about how student referendum results are shared with the relevant departments.
## Apps and Alerts

Officers at the meeting also walked students through the department's own digital tools. NUPD officer Ryan Janusz said the SafeZone app connects users straight to campus police and, when location sharing is on, lets officers see where a caller is, the paper reported. Its emergency button routes to dispatch like a 911 call. The department also uses the Rave system for mass emergency notifications.
Galindo urged students to act as the department's eyes and ears and to report anything that seems wrong, according to the Huntington News.
Federal immigration enforcement has repeatedly reached into the Boston area this fall, and federal judges in Boston have ordered the release of a string of detainees, Universal Hub has reported.

title: Tip Jar Theft at South End Bakery Ends in Foot Chase and Two Injured Officers
dek: Police say a Brockton man who took a tip jar from Tatte Bakery on Harrison Avenue fought officers who caught him two and a half hours later, sending two of them to the hospital.
body: It began as a snatch-and-run at a bakery counter on a Sunday afternoon. By nightfall, Boston police say, it had turned into a foot chase across the South End, a struggle on the pavement near the expressway and two officers on their way to the hospital.

Kobe Nevels, 28, of Brockton, was arraigned Monday, Oct. 19, in Boston Municipal Court on charges of larceny from a building, assault and battery on a police officer and resisting arrest, according to Universal Hub.
## The Theft

At about 5:06 p.m. on Sunday, Oct. 18, officers from District D-4 were sent to a report of a larceny in progress at 345 Harrison Ave., the address of Tatte Bakery, the Boston Police Department said in a release. Staff told the responding officer that a man had taken the tip jar.
The man left, but police say he soon returned to a nearby CVS. Officers searched the area without finding him and broadcast his description to cruisers throughout the district.
## The Chase

About two and a half hours later, at roughly 7:30 p.m., officers patrolling near West Fourth Street and Frontage Road, on the other side of the expressway, saw a man who matched the description, according to the department.

When officers approached, police say, he ran. Several officers caught up with him. According to the police account, he flailed his arms and actively resisted as officers repeatedly ordered him to stop, before they were able to get him into handcuffs.
Two officers were hurt in the struggle. Both were taken to local hospitals with injuries police described as not life-threatening.
## In Court

At Monday's arraignment, Judge Paul Treseler ordered Nevels held at the Suffolk County jail in lieu of $250 bail, Universal Hub reported. As a condition of release if he posts bail, he is ordered to stay away from Tatte.
Police did not say how much money was in the tip jar or whether it was recovered.
District D-4 covers the South End, Back Bay and Fenway. Neither the police release nor the court report included a statement from Nevels or a defense attorney.
The charges are allegations. Nevels is presumed innocent unless and until he is proven guilty.

title: GOP Lieutenant Governor Nominee Shawn Oliver Quits the Race After Drunk-Driving Crash
dek: New Bedford police say the Republican nominee crashed into five parked cars and overturned his vehicle, and his own running mate called on him to step aside 16 days before the election.
body: Sixteen days before Election Day, the Republican Party's candidate for lieutenant governor of Massachusetts is out of the race. Shawn Oliver, a New Bedford city councilor, suspended his campaign on Sunday, Oct. 18, after he was charged with drunken driving, GBH News reported.

According to the New Bedford Police Department, as reported by GBH, Oliver crashed into five parked vehicles and overturned his car late Saturday night. Police took him to St. Luke's Hospital, where he was arrested and charged.

He faces charges of operating under the influence of liquor, negligent operation of a motor vehicle, a marked lanes violation and speeding, GBH reported. The charges are allegations, and no court outcome had been reported as of Sunday.
## A Statement and a Rebuke

Oliver announced the suspension in a statement released Sunday afternoon. According to GBH, he said the election was too important to be overshadowed by personal matters and asked that his family's privacy be respected.

The pressure to step aside came from the top of his own ticket. Mike Minogue, the Republican nominee for governor, had called on Oliver to suspend his campaign immediately, GBH reported. Minogue said he was "extremely disappointed."
> "Shawn is a father and grandfather, and he needs to put his family first." — Mike Minogue, Republican nominee for governor

Minogue also used his Sunday statement to turn the episode toward Gov. Maura Healey. "That starts with accountability, something Massachusetts has not seen from Maura Healey," he said, according to GBH.
## An Unlikely Path to the Ballot

Oliver's spot on the ticket was itself the product of an unusual year. A longtime corrections officer who was born and raised in New Bedford, he won the city's Ward 3 council seat in February 2023, WBUR reported in September, citing State House News Service.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Brian Shortsleeve chose Oliver as his running mate in March. Then the field around him collapsed. According to WBUR, Minogue-backed candidate Anne Brensley failed to meet the ballot signature threshold after a fraudulent signature-gathering problem, and Anne Manning Martin was removed from the ballot over fraudulent signatures after a complaint from Oliver. That left Oliver as the only Republican still running for lieutenant governor, and he won the primary on Sept. 1.
Shortsleeve lost the governor's primary to Minogue, which left Oliver paired with a running mate he had not chosen. Oliver called for party unity after the primary, WBUR reported.
## One Week Earlier, on the Debate Stage

Less than a week before the crash, Oliver faced Democratic Lt. Gov. Kim Driscoll in the only lieutenant governor debate of the campaign, held live on GBH's "Boston Public Radio," according to WBUR and State House News Service.

In that debate, Oliver argued that the Healey administration had hurt the state by refusing to work with President Donald Trump, and he called for collaboration with federal law enforcement on immigration. Speaking about the multiday surge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests in his home city last month, he said "Nobody should be in fear of coming out of their house," WBUR reported. He described himself as a "pro-choice Republican" and the child of an immigrant mother from the Azores.
He also described a "new friendship" with Minogue. "We are in constant communication," he said, according to WBUR.
## What Happens Now

Mail-in voting is already underway. More than 600,000 mail-in ballots had been sent out by the week of Oct. 15, with another 300,000 awaiting delivery, according to Secretary of the Commonwealth Bill Galvin's office, as reported by WBUR. In-person early voting began Saturday, Oct. 17, the same day as the crash.

GBH's report did not say whether the Massachusetts Republican Party would seek to replace Oliver on the ballot, or whether that is possible this close to the Nov. 3 election. Healey and Driscoll are seeking a second term.

title: Two Women Shot on Davison Street as Gunfire Keeps Hitting Hyde Park
dek: The early-morning shooting on Oct. 17 made the women the eighth and ninth people shot in Hyde Park since August, three of them fatally, according to Universal Hub.
body: The calls came in around 1:10 a.m. Saturday, Oct. 17. Two women had been shot outside 114 Davison St., near Arlington Street in Hyde Park, Universal Hub reported. One of them suffered life-threatening injuries, according to WHDH as cited by Universal Hub.
Police had not publicly named the women, described a motive or announced an arrest as of the weekend. The condition of the second woman was not reported.

The shooting extended a run of gun violence in a neighborhood that has long sat at the quieter edge of the city's crime map. By Universal Hub's count, the two women were the eighth and ninth people shot in Hyde Park since August. Three of those victims died.
## Three Killings in Ten Weeks

The first came in the early hours of Aug. 3, outside Little Haiti International Cuisine at 1184 Hyde Park Ave. Boston police responded to gunfire just after 12:30 a.m. and found five adults with gunshot wounds, Boston 25 News reported. Ky Mani Korey Reynolds, 26, died at a hospital. The other four survived.

Oliver Derima, 27, of Randolph, was charged with murder and unlawful possession of a firearm and was ordered held without bail after pleading not guilty in the West Roxbury Division of Boston Municipal Court, according to Boston 25 News. Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said the shooting showed "an utter disregard for the sanctity of life," the station reported.

On Sept. 26, a little after 1 p.m., police were called to a business at 54 Walter St., near the Fairmount commuter rail station. They found Michael Lorenus, 37, of Milton, with multiple gunshot wounds, and he was pronounced dead at the scene, Boston 25 News reported. Universal Hub reported that the building is listed as a marijuana grow facility, and that police were searching for two men seen running outbound along the Fairmount Line tracks. An officer found a gun magazine near the Fairmount Avenue bridge, according to the site. No arrest in that killing had been reported.

On Oct. 7, shortly after 5 p.m., 20-year-old Darryl Aleo was shot inside the Akiki gas station at 1171 Hyde Park Ave., across the street from the restaurant where Reynolds was killed. He died at a hospital. An 18-year-old, Christian Peebles, turned himself in two days later and pleaded not guilty to murder, according to the Boston Globe and Boston.com.
## Questions on the Avenue

The Hyde Park Avenue killings drew sharp reaction from residents in the comment threads under Universal Hub's coverage, where some argued that police should be walking the avenue more often. Universal Hub editor Adam Gaffin responded that having a police station nearby does not by itself reduce crime.

The Boston Licensing Board has also been watching the corridor. After the Aug. 3 shooting, the board first ordered Little Haiti International Cuisine closed, then let it reopen with a 9:30 p.m. closing time instead of 1 a.m. after the owner discussed security plans with police, Universal Hub reported. At a hearing in mid-October, board members questioned the owner about a July 5 visit in which a police sergeant found people inside with music playing at 3 a.m. The owner said they were relatives from Connecticut who were afraid to leave after reports of July 4 shootings in Boston. No sanction had been decided at the time of the hearing.
## Where to Call

Boston police ask anyone with information on the Davison Street shooting or the Hyde Park homicides to call detectives at 617-343-4470. Anonymous tips can go to CrimeStoppers at 1-800-494-TIPS or by texting TIP to CRIME (27463). The Boston Neighborhood Trauma Team offers free support 24 hours a day at 617-431-0125.

title: Federal Judges in Boston Keep Ordering ICE to Let People Go
dek: In one week, a judge gave ICE a 3 p.m. deadline to free a Cuban electrician held ten months, and another intervened for a Provincetown police employee locked in a cell at Logan for 44 hours.
body: The order landed shortly before 9 a.m. on Thursday, Oct. 16. U.S. District Judge Leo Sorokin gave Immigration and Customs Enforcement until 3 p.m. that same day to release Yasmani Toyo Lara, a Cuban national the agency had held since December 2025, Universal Hub reported.

Toyo Lara had spent about ten months in custody at the Plymouth County jail, nearly six of them after his removal order became final, according to Universal Hub. He was separated from his American wife, his children, his mother and his job as a union electrician.
## Nowhere to Send Him

ICE had tried to deport him and failed. Cuba refused to take him, reportedly because of his 2018 Connecticut convictions for burglary and assault and because of tensions with the U.S. government, Universal Hub reported. Mexico also refused, saying it accepts only immigrants who agree to go there. Toyo Lara did not agree.

Government lawyers told the court they were "actively" searching for a third country. Sorokin wrote that the claim was "unsupported by any specific facts," noting the government had named no country and no timeline, according to Universal Hub.

Relying on the 2001 Supreme Court decision in Zadvydas v. Davis, which sets six months as the presumptive limit for detaining immigrants who cannot be removed, Sorokin found that Toyo Lara's removal "is not significantly likely to occur in the reasonably foreseeable future." His continued detention, the judge wrote, was "unreasonable, and he must be released." The order releases him under supervision and does not stop ICE from continuing to look for a country that will accept him, Universal Hub reported.
## Forty-Four Hours at Terminal E
A week earlier, another federal judge in Boston stepped in on behalf of a 21-year-old who never meant to leave the country.

Carlos Maldonado Valle, a Cape Cod Community College criminal justice student who works part-time and volunteers with the Provincetown Police Department, was flying home from a vacation in Puerto Rico when another passenger had a medical emergency, GBH News reported. The plane diverted to Bermuda. That stop turned a domestic trip into an international arrival, and the flight landed at Logan Airport's Terminal E.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection officers asked whether he was a U.S. citizen. He told them he was from Honduras. He was held in secondary screening from about 4:30 p.m. Tuesday, Oct. 6, according to an emergency habeas petition described by GBH, and spent 44 hours alone in a cell, eating only snack food, with his phone and ID taken. He told GBH he had repeated panic attacks.
> "The moment they said that I was going to go back to Honduras, my heart dropped and I couldn't breathe." — Carlos Maldonado Valle, to GBH News

On the evening of Oct. 7, U.S. District Judge Julia E. Kobick barred federal authorities from removing him from the country or moving him out of Massachusetts for at least 72 hours, GBH reported. He was released on Oct. 8 after paying $1,020 to be paroled into the country. Maldonado Valle came to the U.S. from Honduras at about age 10 and holds Special Immigrant Juvenile protection approved Oct. 1, according to GBH, and his attorney, Rachel Self, said he has no criminal record.

Provincetown Town Manager Alex Morse and Police Chief Gregory Hennick wrote letters supporting his release. "I was shocked and scared for him," Hennick told GBH. CBP and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to GBH's questions.
## Arrested Outside a Police Station

Not every case ended with a release. Universal Hub, citing GBH, reported on Oct. 8 that Melanie Tinoco Camacho, an Ecuadorian native, was detained by four men who were not in uniform as she walked out of Boston Police District 4 in the South End. Her American husband, Martin Gurfinkiel, who had come to pick her up, said the men did not identify who they worked for. She was being held at ICE's Burlington facility at the time of the report.

A Boston police spokesperson has said that immigration status is not a factor for officers and that they do not ask about it, as quoted in a reader comment on Universal Hub's report. Whether the department shared any information about her release with federal agents was not addressed in the coverage.

title: Suspicious Letters Reach Five Massachusetts Members of Congress and the State Elections Office
dek: The FBI and Postal Inspection Service are investigating a nationwide wave of mailings, some containing an unknown substance, sent to election and congressional offices three weeks before Election Day.
body: Three weeks before Election Day, envelopes flagged as potentially hazardous began turning up at political offices across Massachusetts. By late Friday, Oct. 16, five members of the state's all-Democratic congressional delegation said their offices had received suspicious letters, and so had the state's Elections Division, GBH News reported.

The FBI's Boston Division said it is investigating with the U.S. Postal Inspection Service a series of suspicious mailings that included letters to secretaries of state and election offices, according to GBH. Some of the letters contained an unknown substance, and investigators were working to identify who sent them.
## The Offices Hit

Reps. Jake Auchincloss, Ayanna Pressley, Stephen Lynch, Seth Moulton and Lori Trahan all reported receiving letters, GBH reported. The mailings appear to have gone to their district offices in Massachusetts rather than to Washington.

A spokesman for Auchincloss said Postal Service inspectors retrieved a suspicious letter sent to his Newton office, and that the office was following guidance from the House Sergeant at Arms. A Pressley spokesperson said her district office received a letter matching the description of those sent elsewhere. Federal and local law enforcement were notified, and the Boston Police Department responded and is investigating, according to GBH.
## The Elections Division

The envelope addressed to the Massachusetts Elections Division arrived Friday morning, WBUR reported. Staff alerted state and federal authorities as soon as they saw it, according to a statement from Secretary of the Commonwealth William Galvin, and the Postal Inspection Service took custody of it. It was not opened, GBH reported.
Galvin credited information from the FBI and Postal Inspection Service with helping his staff spot the envelope before it reached the office.
> "The Elections Division's work was uninterrupted." — Secretary of the Commonwealth William Galvin, as quoted by WBUR

WBUR reported that it was unclear whether the envelope sent to Galvin's office contained a powder. A spokesperson for Gov. Maura Healey said she had not received a letter, according to GBH. Healey praised the state and federal response and called for those responsible to be held accountable.
## A National Pattern

The investigation first surfaced in a Thursday message from the Senate Sergeant at Arms to Senate offices, which warned that some letters might still be in transit, GBH and the Associated Press reported. U.S. Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester, Alex Padilla and Kirsten Gillibrand reported suspicious mail intercepted before it reached their offices.

Packages containing powder forced evacuations of election offices in Louisiana and Oklahoma during the same week, according to GBH and the AP. Ohio's secretary of state said the Postal Service intercepted a package with white powder. In Wisconsin, the Elections Commission said tests showed the powder it received was not hazardous.

The National Association of Secretaries of State and the National Association of State Election Directors condemned the threats, saying election workers "should never fear for their safety" while doing their jobs, GBH reported.
The mailings echo a 2023 incident in which election offices in six states received white-powder letters, some carrying threats and traces of fentanyl, according to GBH and the AP.
## The Election Calendar

Massachusetts voters are already casting ballots. In-person early voting began Saturday, Oct. 17, and hundreds of thousands of mail-in ballots have been sent out, WBUR reported. Galvin's office said the Elections Division's work was not disrupted, and no injuries tied to the Massachusetts letters were reported in the coverage.

title: Healey and Minogue Trade Blows Over Accountability, ICE and Costs in Final Debate
dek: The last televised debate of the governor's race turned on a fired aide's arrest, a State Police scandal and the federal immigration crackdown.
body: The final debate of the Massachusetts governor's race was not a polite one. Gov. Maura Healey and Republican challenger Mike Minogue met Thursday night, Oct. 15, at WCVB's studio in Needham, and fought over affordability, immigration and who should answer for the state's recent scandals, according to WBUR, NBC Boston and Boston.com.

The debate was hosted by WCVB, WBUR and the Boston Globe, with El Planeta and the Bay State Banner, WBUR reported. Independent candidate Andrea James, who has polled in the low single digits, was not invited.
## "In the Real World"

Minogue, a first-time candidate and former CEO of medical device maker Abiomed, came in pressing on accountability, Boston.com reported. His sharpest material arrived the day before the debate, when federal prosecutors arrested LaMar Cook, Healey's former deputy director for Western Massachusetts, on SNAP and wire fraud charges. Cook had already been charged in October 2025 with cocaine trafficking and firearm offenses.

Healey said she fired Cook immediately. Minogue's reply, as reported by Boston.com: "If someone's arrested, they're automatically fired in the real world." He also criticized the roughly $22,000 Cook was paid for unused vacation time, according to NBC Boston and State House News Service. After the debate, Healey said, "I wish I never hired LaMar Cook," NBC Boston reported.
## "Sometimes Things Happen"

The candidates also clashed over a State Police internal affairs case in which a civilian, reportedly invited by a trooper to stay overnight at a barracks on Martha's Vineyard, is accused of raping a woman there, according to NBC Boston. Healey defended State Police Col. Geoffrey Noble.
> "Sometimes things happen, but I can tell you, he and I make sure that swift action is taken." — Gov. Maura Healey, as quoted by NBC Boston

Minogue answered that "sometimes things happen" is not acceptable, and said "a woman was raped," WBUR reported. Healey noted that the man accused is a civilian, not a trooper, according to Boston.com.
## ICE and the Federal Fight

Healey tied her opponent repeatedly to President Donald Trump, mentioning Trump 13 times, by WBUR's count. On immigration, she defended limits on state cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "The problem is ICE," she said, according to WBUR, adding that people are afraid to go to school because of the agency.

Minogue said he would work with ICE to remove criminals and urged leaders to "lower the temperature," WBUR reported. He argued that coordination between local, state and federal authorities helps stop drug dealers, according to Boston.com.
## Gas Taxes, Pipelines and Permits

Both candidates support suspending the state gas tax, though they differ on how long, NBC Boston reported. Minogue blamed Healey's opposition to natural gas pipelines for high utility bills and proposed cutting utility fees by a third. Healey backed what she called an "all of the above" energy approach and said Minogue "will kill wind right now," according to Boston.com.

On housing, Minogue said Massachusetts is last in the nation for building permits per person and proposed 45-day permit timelines, WBUR reported. Healey said the state has already cut state permit review to 30 days, and cited 100,000 homes built or in development.

On abortion, Minogue, who describes himself as pro-life, said he would follow state law but did not say whether he supports a 2028 ballot effort to repeal a law easing restrictions after 24 weeks, NBC Boston reported. "I trust women and their doctors. Mike Minogue doesn't," Healey said, according to Boston.com. Minogue called her line a "cheap shot," WBUR reported.
## The State of the Race

Polls by MassINC Polling and the UNH Survey Center in September showed Healey with more than 50% support and Minogue below 40%, according to WBUR. UMass Boston political scientist Paul Watanabe told WBUR that Minogue "proved to be more than just his ads" but did not lay out a broader agenda.
Minogue closed by calling the election a "tipping point," NBC Boston reported. The election is Nov. 3.

title: Suspect in Random Allston Triple Stabbing Sent to Bridgewater for Competency Exam
dek: One victim says the knife stopped a millimeter from his jugular; the Brighton man charged in the attack was arrested days later swinging a machete, police say.
body: One moment they were out on a Saturday night in Allston. The next, a stranger was stabbing them. Shortly before 1:30 a.m. on Sunday, Oct. 4, three men were attacked near Cambridge Street and Highgate Street, Universal Hub and Boston.com reported. One was stabbed in the back, one in the neck and one slashed across the face.

Boston EMS took all three to local hospitals, and police said their injuries were not considered life-threatening, according to Boston.com. The attacker rode away on an e-bike, Universal Hub reported, citing Staco City.
## "One Millimeter Away"

One of the victims, Noah Walsh, later described the attack in a post on his Substack, which Universal Hub summarized on Oct. 16. Walsh wrote that he looked down and saw a knife lodged in his neck, held by a man he had never seen. He collapsed, drifted in and out of consciousness for about two hours, and woke up in the trauma unit at Mass General Brigham, where a CT scan showed the blade had stopped "one millimeter away from my jugular vein."
One of his friends was stabbed in the back, puncturing a lung, and another suffered a large gash to the face, according to Walsh's account as reported by Universal Hub.
> "I refuse to let what happened to my friends and me become just another statistic." — Noah Walsh, stabbing victim, as quoted by Universal Hub
Walsh asked how such an attack could happen in a city that sees itself as progressive and safe, and whether it could have been prevented, Universal Hub reported.
## A Machete on Western Avenue

Police made an arrest four days later, after a separate call. Shortly before 5 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 8, officers responded to reports of a man swinging a large knife near Leo M. Birmingham Parkway and Waverly Street in Brighton, according to Boston.com and Universal Hub.

Officers did not find him at the scene but located him several blocks away on Western Avenue, Universal Hub reported. Police said he dropped the weapon when detectives ordered him to. Officers recovered a large machete from the sidewalk and found a folding knife with reddish-brown stains in his right front pants pocket, according to police as reported by Universal Hub.
The man was identified as Joshua Flores, 24, of Brighton. He was first charged with carrying a dangerous weapon and disturbing the peace.
"After further investigation, detectives developed probable cause to charge Flores with a recent triple stabbing," Boston police said, according to Boston.com.
## The Charges

In the Allston attack, Flores faces three counts of armed assault with intent to murder, three counts of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon causing serious bodily injury, and two counts of mayhem, Boston.com and Universal Hub reported. The charges are allegations, and Flores is presumed innocent.
At his arraignment, Brighton Municipal Court Judge Shelley Joseph ordered him held without bail pending a dangerousness hearing, according to Boston.com.
## Sent for Evaluation

That hearing was scheduled for Oct. 15. Instead of ruling on dangerousness, Judge Connie Wong ordered Flores sent to Bridgewater State Hospital for an evaluation of his competency to stand trial, Universal Hub reported. He is due back in court on Nov. 3.
Boston.com reported that it was not clear whether Flores had an attorney. Police have not described a motive, and Walsh's account describes the attacker as a stranger.

title: Boston's After-Hours Fight: Smashburgers, Nip Bottles and a $600,000 Liquor License
dek: In one week, the Licensing Board split the difference on a 2 a.m. burger counter in South Boston and shut down nips in Allston, as the state auditor called for scrapping liquor-license caps.
body: Boston still goes to bed early, and this week the city's Licensing Board made sure of it. Over two days in mid-October, the board heard a fight over late-night smashburgers in South Boston, rejected small liquor bottles in Allston, and grilled a Hyde Park bar owner about a 3 a.m. party, Universal Hub reported. At the same time, State Auditor Diana DiZoglio released a report arguing that the system that makes a Boston liquor license cost up to $600,000 should be torn down, according to WBUR.
## "We Do Sleep Here in Boston"

7th Street Burger, a New York take-out smashburger chain that opened at 475 West Broadway in Perkins Square in April, asked to push its closing time from 11 p.m. to 2 a.m., Universal Hub reported. Residents and City Councilor Ed Flynn opposed it.

Silver Street resident Ellen Fritch told the board she already struggles to sleep after midnight because of loud bar patrons. "New York is the city that doesn't sleep," she said, "but we do sleep here in Boston," according to Universal Hub. Another resident, Amanda Jerome, pointed to wrapper litter and scooter-riding delivery drivers. Flynn, speaking through an aide, cited noise, pedestrian safety and pest control.

The company's attorney, Tom Miller, said the chain typically stays open until 3 or 4 a.m. at other locations without problems, serves shift workers, students and hotel guests, and has no seats, so customers do not linger, Universal Hub reported. Chairwoman Kathleen Joyce called the company a good operator but said she was worried about congestion on Broadway at bar closing.

On Oct. 15, the board settled on 1 a.m., a compromise the business itself offered after the hearing, according to Universal Hub. It cannot come back seeking 2 a.m. for at least a year. Joyce said she wanted the business to "build trust with the neighbors."

The same hearing included a request by Achilitos Taqueria to take over the former Little Stevie's space on Boylston Street in the Fenway with hours until 2 a.m. most nights and 2:30 a.m. on weekends. It drew no opposition, Universal Hub reported.
## No Nips on Comm. Ave.

In Allston, Commonwealth Cellars at 1229 Commonwealth Ave., near Harvard Avenue, asked to sell nip-sized liquor bottles. The board rejected it with prejudice on Oct. 15, meaning owner Wondimu Abeje must wait at least a year to try again, Universal Hub reported.

Conor Newman, deputy director of the Mayor's Office of Neighborhood Services, argued that public drinking in Allston Village is an ongoing problem that nip sales would make worse. The Allston Civic Association also opposed the request. "I don't think it makes sense in this particular area," Joyce said, according to Universal Hub.
## The 3 a.m. Birthday

The board also questioned George Craan, owner of Little Haiti International Cuisine at 1184 Hyde Park Ave., about a July 5 visit in which a police sergeant found people inside with music playing at 3 a.m., Universal Hub reported. Craan said about 15 relatives from Connecticut, celebrating a 50th birthday, were afraid to leave separately after reports of July 4 shootings. "Your name is on this license," Joyce told him. The bar's hours had already been cut to 9:30 p.m. after a fatal shooting outside on Aug. 3.
## The Auditor's Case

DiZoglio's 181-page report says Massachusetts' population-based caps on liquor licenses create artificial scarcity, WBUR reported. Licenses cost up to $600,000 in Boston and $175,000 in Somerville, but about $2,500 in Cambridge, which controls its own licensing, according to the report. Local-control communities issued twice as many licenses per capita as capped ones.

"We need a liquor licensing system that is transparent, fair and gives all of our local businesses a shot at success," DiZoglio said, according to WBUR. Steve Clark of the Massachusetts Restaurant Association said owners treat licenses as valuable assets and suggested a buyback program. Language eliminating the caps is in the Senate's economic development bill, still in negotiation; Gov. Maura Healey supports removing them, while some House leaders have raised concerns, WBUR reported.

title: Former Healey Aide LaMar Cook Jailed After Federal SNAP Fraud Arrest
dek: Already awaiting trial on cocaine trafficking charges, the governor's ex-deputy for Western Massachusetts is accused of collecting food aid while hiding income, and a judge revoked his bail.
body: LaMar Cook was already awaiting trial on cocaine trafficking and gun charges. This week, federal prosecutors added fraud, and a state judge sent him back to jail, according to WBUR, Axios Boston and Boston.com.

Cook, 46, of Springfield, was Gov. Maura Healey's deputy director for Western Massachusetts until he was fired in October 2025, when the drug and gun charges were announced, WBUR reported. Investigators allegedly intercepted eight kilograms of cocaine scheduled for delivery to the state office building where he worked, according to Boston.com. He pleaded not guilty and was released on $25,000 bail in March.
## The Federal Case
On Wednesday, Oct. 14, U.S. Attorney Leah Foley's office charged Cook with one count each of SNAP fraud and wire fraud, Axios Boston reported.

Prosecutors allege Cook applied for Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits on April 6, reporting no income and $100 in the bank, when at least one of his accounts held more than $8,800, WBUR reported. He has allegedly received more than $500 a month in benefits since then.

According to prosecutors, as reported by WBUR and Axios, Cook's application listed only his child as a household member, though he lived with his fiancée, a Springfield Public Schools employee earning more than $80,000 a year, and her mother. A USDA special agent wrote that her income "should have been disclosed," Axios reported.

Prosecutors also allege that around the time he was collecting benefits, Cook received about $12,000 in Zelle payments from his mother, who had recently won $1 million in the state lottery, and $2,497.88 in tax refunds, WBUR reported. He allegedly used his EBT card for groceries during a July trip to Florida and spent $1,904 on flights to Orlando for eight people, according to Axios.
> "I find it disturbing that the Commonwealth of Massachusetts could not prevent this from happening." — U.S. Attorney Leah Foley, as quoted by WBUR
Foley called Cook's alleged conduct "egregious," WBUR reported. The charges are allegations; Cook has not been convicted.
## The Vacation Payout

The federal complaint arrives on top of a separate fight over money Cook received after he was fired. He was paid his $130,227 salary and $22,374.29 in accrued vacation pay, WBUR reported. The state later called the vacation payout an error but could not recover it because his account lacked the funds, and Attorney General Andrea Campbell sued in January to get it back.

In a Facebook post addressing the coverage, Cook used the phrase "welfare golden parachute" and described the money as a mix of earned vacation pay, his mother's lottery winnings and an EBT card, according to Axios.
## Back Behind Bars

Cook appeared in Boston federal court on Wednesday and was released on personal recognizance, Boston.com reported. The next day, Hampden County prosecutors went to state court to revoke his bail in the drug case, arguing the new charges violated a release condition requiring him to obey federal law.

"We're here because Mr. Cook committed more crimes," Hampden County District Attorney Kerry Beattie said, according to Boston.com. Defense attorney Kedar Ismail argued the federal charges were only allegations. "This is some type of stretch," he said. Judge David Hodge revoked Cook's bail and ordered him held for 90 days.
## The Political Fallout

The arrest landed one day before the final governor's debate. Healey said the program is federal and that she was glad the U.S. attorney's office was prosecuting, Axios reported. Republican nominee Mike Minogue said "there was no accountability." On the debate stage, Healey said she fired Cook immediately; afterward she said, "I wish I never hired LaMar Cook," NBC Boston reported.

title: The Fight Over Blue Hill Avenue: Boston Pushes Ahead on Center Bus Lanes Despite Protests
dek: The Wu administration is moving forward with a $163 million redesign that would put bus-only lanes down the middle of Blue Hill Avenue, even as a city councilor, a state representative and some business owners push back.
body: Blue Hill Avenue runs through the heart of Mattapan, Dorchester and Roxbury, and for years residents have complained about its traffic, its dangerous crossings and its crawling buses. Now the plan to fix it has become a political fight of its own.

The city is moving ahead with plans for center-running bus lanes along about three miles of the avenue, WBUR reported on Oct. 15, despite a wave of opposition from some elected officials and residents.
## The Plan

The lanes are part of a roughly $163 million overhaul of Blue Hill Avenue between Mattapan Square and Grove Hall, according to WBUR. Federal grants would cover more than half the cost; most recently, the city secured $80 million in March.

Two lanes in the middle of the road would be reserved for buses and emergency vehicles. Bus stops would move from the sidewalks to concrete platforms in the center of the street. The plan also includes new crosswalks, signals and sidewalks, new trees and 42 parking spaces.

At a Sept. 30 public meeting, Wu said the design would nearly cut bus travel time on the corridor in half, with buses arriving every three to six minutes, WBUR reported. Interim Chief of Streets Chris Osgood said the plan reflects resident feedback gathered since 2019.

The city is about a third of the way through design. Officials hope to show updated plans before December, and construction would not start before 2028 and could take up to three years, according to WBUR.
## The Opposition

Before the Sept. 30 town hall, state Rep. Christopher Worrell helped organize a protest of about a dozen people at the Grove Hall Mecca, WBUR reported. He argued that moving bus stops to the middle of the street would force riders, including children and seniors, to cross two lanes of traffic to reach them.

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who represents District 7 in Roxbury, opposes the center lanes and wants the city and the MBTA to consider extending the Orange Line instead. In September his office announced a trip to Washington to press the idea with the Senate Banking Committee and the offices of Sen. Elizabeth Warren and Rep. Ayanna Pressley, Universal Hub reported. He and District 4 Councilor Brian Worrell have proposed an Orange Line branch running from Ruggles toward Mattapan Square.
Universal Hub noted that when the elevated Washington Street line was torn down in the 1980s, Roxbury was promised comparable rapid-transit service that never came.

Peter Papadogiannis, who has owned Boulevard Cleaners in Mattapan since the early 1980s, told WBUR he fears that parking competition and construction will drive customers away, and that he might have to close within months of work starting. A Change.org petition opposes the center lanes.
## The Supporters

Transit advocates have issued a joint statement backing the design. Katarina Torres-Radisic of Transportation for Massachusetts told WBUR the plan would shorten bus trips and make the corridor fully accessible to people with disabilities for the first time. Resident Grace Richardson thanked the mayor for addressing what she described as historical disinvestment in Boston's Black community.
The latest round of public comment on the design closed the week of Oct. 12, according to WBUR.

sources.title: Amid pushback, Boston moves ahead with Blue Hill Ave. center bus lanes project
Mr. Culpepper goes to Washington to press for extending the Orange Line down Blue Hill Avenue

title: Two Plead Guilty in the 2023 Mass and Cass Stabbing Death of Kimberly Webb
dek: Michael Bellanti and Crystal Morgan avoided first-degree murder trials by pleading to manslaughter in the killing of a 39-year-old mother of three.
body: Three years after Kimberly Webb was stabbed on a South End street at the edge of Mass and Cass, the two people charged with killing her have pleaded guilty, according to Boston.com and Universal Hub. Both were originally charged with murder. Both took manslaughter deals instead.

Michael Bellanti, 35, pleaded guilty to manslaughter in Suffolk Superior Court on Tuesday, Oct. 13, just as his first-degree murder trial was set to begin, Universal Hub reported. Judge James Budreau sentenced him to 10 to 15 years at the Souza Baranowski Correctional Center, with a little more than three years of credit for time already served.

Crystal Morgan, 41, was scheduled to start her own first-degree murder trial the next day. Instead, on Wednesday morning, Oct. 14, she also pleaded guilty to manslaughter and was sentenced to six to eight years in state prison, Boston.com and Universal Hub reported. Universal Hub identified the judge in her case as Christopher Belezos.
## What Prosecutors Say Happened

The Suffolk County District Attorney's Office laid out the case in court filings described by Boston.com and Universal Hub. The killing began as an argument among the three on Aug. 18, 2023, near Atkinson Street. Boston police officers broke up the fight and sent them in opposite directions.

Webb walked toward Southampton and Topeka streets, prosecutors said. Bellanti and Morgan took a route that brought them back onto Topeka. Bellanti bent down and retrieved an item from near his right sock, then approached Webb with Morgan following, according to the DA's account.

Prosecutors said Morgan held Webb's arm to keep her from leaving while Bellanti backed her across the street and stabbed her in the chest, hand and arm. "Bellanti begins slashing and stabbing in the direction of Webb," the DA's office wrote, according to Universal Hub. The two then walked off toward Southampton Street.
Webb made her way back toward Atkinson Street and was taken to a hospital. She died nine days later, Boston.com reported.
## "A Smile That Lit Up a Room"
Webb was 39, a mother of three and the caretaker for her mother, who uses a wheelchair, according to Boston.com. She had been struggling with the death of her sister.
Her best friend of more than three decades, whose name was not published, read a victim impact statement in court, Boston.com reported.
> "We had hope that she would get through this difficult time, get help, find sobriety, and rebuild her life." — Kimberly Webb's best friend, in a statement read in court, as reported by Boston.com
The friend described Webb as "absolutely hilarious" with "a smile that lit up a room," according to Boston.com.
## The Deal

Court filings show the murder charges were reduced to manslaughter under plea agreements, Boston.com reported. Defense attorneys Dmitry Lev, representing Bellanti, and Daniel P. Fitzgerald, representing Morgan, did not respond to Boston.com's requests for comment.

Bellanti will serve his sentence at Souza Baranowski, according to Universal Hub. With credit for more than three years already spent in custody awaiting trial, his minimum term is already partly served.

title: Boston Book Festival Takes Over Copley Square With Emily Wilson and More Than 50 Authors
dek: The free 18th annual Boston Book Festival set up in and around Copley Square on Saturday, Oct. 17, with translator Emily Wilson as keynote speaker.
body: For one Saturday in October, the stone heart of the Back Bay turns into an open-air reading room. The Boston Book Festival returned to Copley Square on Oct. 17 for its 18th year, with more than 50 authors, more than 70 vendors and every session free, according to WBUR.

Panels were scheduled across the square's institutions: the Boston Public Library's Copley Square building, Old South Church and the Goethe-Institut. More than 25,000 people attended last year, WBUR reported.
## No Tickets, by Design

Executive director Carlin Carr told WBUR that keeping every session open to the public lets people wander into talks they would never have bought a ticket for. She described the festival as a beloved city tradition, run in partnership with the Boston Public Library.
The lineup spanned fiction, nonfiction, poetry and young adult writing.
## The Keynote

The keynote speaker was Emily Wilson, the classicist whose translations of Homer's The Odyssey and The Iliad have reached readers far outside academia. She last appeared at the festival in 2023, WBUR reported.

Wilson came with a new book, Crossing the Wine-Dark Sea: Journeys Through Ancient Literature, a collection of essays about the problems of carrying ancient texts into modern language. According to WBUR, she wrote it for readers with little background in translation or in Greek and Roman literature, as a guide to a range of ancient poets, philosophers and authors and to how later generations have received them.
## A Dorchester Son Returns

Howard Bryant, the journalist and author who grew up in Dorchester and now lives in Amherst, returned for his fourth festival appearance, according to WBUR. His book, Kings and Pawns: Jackie Robinson and Paul Robeson in America, follows the two Black American figures and their careers through the Cold War.
Bryant was booked on a panel titled How to Be a Citizen alongside Roger Berkowitz and Eric Liu. His sister, the writer Tisa Bryant, was also on the author list.
## Parades, Free Books and Food Trucks
The day opened with a children's costume parade inside the library, inspired by Eleanor Davis's picture book A Very Good Parade, followed by a storytime hosted by Davis herself, WBUR reported.

Reading Is Fundamental, the national literacy nonprofit, planned to give away free books to mark its 60th anniversary. Organizers also expanded the food offerings with more food trucks and a coffee cart.
The festival fell on the same weekend as the Head of the Charles Regatta, which WBUR also previewed, putting two of Boston's signature fall crowds on the move within a few miles of each other.

title: HubSpot Cuts 660 Jobs, and a Cofounder's One-Line Farewell Draws a Public Apology
dek: Cambridge software company HubSpot announced about 660 layoffs, roughly 7 percent of its workforce, and cofounder Dharmesh Shah later apologized for a LinkedIn post about the cuts that critics called cold.
body: On Tuesday, Oct. 6, HubSpot, the marketing-software company headquartered in Cambridge, told nearly 660 of its employees their jobs were being eliminated.

Chief executive Yamini Rangan announced the cuts, about 7 percent of the workforce, in a letter to employees, Boston.com reported. A week later, one of the company's two founders was publicly apologizing for how he said goodbye.
## The Cuts

HubSpot, which was founded in 2006 by MIT graduate students Brian Halligan and Dharmesh Shah, has more than 9,000 employees, about 306,000 customers and 15 offices worldwide, according to Boston.com. The company did not say how many of the eliminated jobs are in Massachusetts.

In her letter, Rangan framed the layoffs as a reorganization rather than belt-tightening. She wrote that the move is not simply about cutting costs, Boston.com reported, and said the reductions were not driven by efficiency gains from new automation technology.

Instead, she said, HubSpot is changing what it sells: moving from building software that helps customers grow to delivering results for them directly. That shift, she wrote, is transforming the company's products, its pricing and how it serves customers.

Product teams will be reorganized around customer outcomes rather than around the company's individual software products, known internally as Hubs, and HubSpot plans to remove layers of management, according to Boston.com.

Departing employees will receive 20 weeks of base pay plus one more week for each year of service, capped at 30 weeks, along with health benefits and six months of career-transition services. They can keep their company laptops and home-office equipment.
## The Post

Shah, HubSpot's cofounder and chief technology officer, has more than 1.2 million followers on LinkedIn. After the layoffs, he posted a brief note thanking departing employees for helping build the company and wishing them well in their next chapter, the Boston Globe reported.
The reaction was split. Some commenters called the message impersonal and out of touch, according to the Globe, while others said it was good that he had acknowledged the layoffs at all.
## The Apology

Shah then added an apology to the post. He wrote that he was sincerely sorry that his original message had been curt and insensitive, the Globe reported, and said that while he had wanted to express gratitude publicly, he had failed to acknowledge the pain and uncertainty of losing a job.
> "I should have showed the people who helped build HubSpot more care and empathy." — Dharmesh Shah

Shah founded the software company Pyramid Digital Solutions, which was acquired in 2005, before starting HubSpot the following year, according to the Globe. He has written widely about startups and marketing.
HubSpot did not say when the job cuts would take effect, according to Boston.com.

HubSpot cofounder apologizes for 'curt and insensitive' post about layoffs

title: Back to Tape: Cambridge's Q Division Studios Revives Its Analog Week
dek: The 40-year-old Cambridge recording studio where the Pixies, Morphine and Aimee Mann once cut tracks to tape spent a week in September recording local bands on a two-inch, 24-track reel-to-reel machine.
body: Two-inch tape costs about $400 a reel, only a handful of companies still make it, and one wrong move can wipe out a take for good. For one week in September, Q Division Studios in Cambridge handed it to local bands for free.

The 40-year-old studio brought back its Analog Tape Week, an event that had been on hold since the pandemic, WBUR reported on Oct. 9. The goal was to introduce musicians, younger ones especially, to recording on reel-to-reel in an era when almost everything is made on a computer, and to take the cost of tape off their hands.
## The Machine

The centerpiece was a Studer 827, a two-inch, 24-track tape machine that main audio tech Michael Healey, 32, dated to roughly the late 1990s. It is the only machine of its kind currently in service at the studio, he told WBUR.

Healey threaded the tape and ran the transport for the sessions. He demonstrated the machine's fast-forward, comparing it to a Walkman, and the engineers played a drum-and-bass track slowed far down and in reverse, effects they said tape handles particularly well.
Q Division has done the bulk of its production on computers since the early 2000s, according to WBUR.
## A Studio With a Past

Head engineer Rafi Sofer, 53, started at Q Division in 2000, when he learned to edit tape. Around that time, WBUR reported, the Pixies, Morphine and Aimee Mann were among the artists recording to analog tape in its rooms.

Sofer told WBUR that tape has a physical character that is hard to define but that he finds appealing. It also changes how people play. Because mistakes are hard to fix, he said, tape demands more preparation from musicians and engineers and raises the stakes of every performance.

Digital editing is non-destructive, with unlimited undo and endless copies. Tape can tear, break or be erased by accident, and those losses can be permanent. Sofer also acknowledged that digital tools have opened up music production to independent artists.
## A Band's First Reel

Among the bands that booked time was a local alt-rock trio that had never recorded on tape as a band: singer and guitarist Sam Coren, 38, bassist JC Climent, 46, and drummer Michael Nasawaty, 47, who had last worked on analog gear more than a decade earlier, WBUR reported.
Starting on a Monday morning, the band rehearsed and tracked a song called "Time Will Tell" on 24-track tape, then gathered in the control room to hear it played back off the reel.
## Next Session
Q Division hopes to hold another Analog Tape Week in January, according to WBUR. The studio had reopened in 2023, a comeback WBUR also covered.

sources.title: Q Division Studios went old-school for a week with reel-to-reel tape

title: Murder Charge Filed in June Mattapan Shooting That Killed One and Wounded Four
dek: A 19-year-old Jamaica Plain man was charged Oct. 7 with first-degree murder in a June 27 shooting outside 1460 Blue Hill Avenue, the fourth person charged in the case.
body: More than three months after a backyard fight in Mattapan turned into a shooting that left a man dead on the sidewalk and four others wounded, prosecutors have charged the man they say pulled the trigger.

Cerrone Wilcox Buford, 19, of Jamaica Plain, was arraigned Wednesday, Oct. 7, in Suffolk Superior Court on charges of first-degree murder, armed assault to murder, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon causing serious bodily injury and several firearm offenses, according to the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office. He was ordered held without bail.
He is the fourth person charged in connection with the June 27 shooting, and the only one charged with murder.
## What Prosecutors Say Happened
According to the district attorney's office, a fight broke out in the backyard of 1460 Blue Hill Avenue and spilled out onto the front sidewalk. Prosecutors say a gunman fired at least seven shots.

Boston 25 News reported that, according to the DA, video and witnesses showed Wilcox Buford pull a gun from a bag and point it at a 26-year-old Brockton man. The man was shot in the head and pronounced dead at the scene.
Four other people were hit by gunfire. Their injuries were not considered life-threatening, Boston 25 reported.
## Three Others Charged
The case has unfolded in stages. Prosecutors said three other men, all of whom were among the wounded, have also been charged, according to Boston 25.

Javen Girault, 23, of Brockton, was the first. He was charged Sept. 28 with carrying a firearm without a license and possessing a large-capacity feeding device, and bail was set at $5,000, the DA's office said.

Laquan Burris, 18, of Dorchester, was charged Oct. 2 with two counts of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon. Prosecutors listed the weapons as a firearm and a shod foot. His bail was set at $100,000.
A warrant has been issued for the arrest of Mannice Mitchner, 19, of Boston, on a charge of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, a shod foot, according to the DA's office.
The fourth wounded person was a 22-year-old man, Boston 25 reported. He has not been charged.
## The DA's Warning

District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement that the case shows the damage illegal guns do, and that his office is working with law enforcement partners to arrest and prosecute everyone responsible.
> "Someone who pulls the trigger once will likely do it again." — Kevin Hayden, Suffolk County District Attorney
## Next in Court
Wilcox Buford, Burris and Girault are due back in Suffolk Superior Court on Nov. 3 for pre-trial hearings, according to prosecutors.
All four men are presumed innocent unless and until they are proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

title: Boston Plans Its First Indigenous Monument on Franklin Park's Scarboro Hill
dek: The White Pine Gathering Place, designed by and for the Wampanoag people, would be the first permanent monument in Boston dedicated to an Indigenous community, city officials say.
body: On a wooded rise in Franklin Park, a circle of white pines, steel poles and benches is meant to one day surround a single pot inscribed with the story of a giant.

The White Pine Gathering Place, planned for Scarboro Hill, would be the first permanent monument in Boston dedicated to an Indigenous community, according to city officials quoted by WBUR. It is being designed by and for the Wampanoag people as a place for ceremony, gathering and healing.
## The Story at the Center

The monument will tell the story of Moshup, a giant in Wampanoag tradition who separated Martha's Vineyard from Cape Cod, WBUR reported. The story will be inscribed on a pot at the center, with benches and Corten steel poles arranged in a circle around it so visitors can read it.

White pine trees, which symbolize life for the Wampanoag, will be planted around the benches. Small statues will depict Pukwudgies, the mischievous but well-meaning little figures of regional folklore.

Community members wanted a monument that honors the land, works for tribal communities and teaches the public, according to WBUR. It is meant for Indigenous and non-Indigenous visitors alike, down to families looking for a place to picnic.
## Who Designed It

The design comes from SmokeSygnals, an organization that builds exhibits and installations about Indigenous history and culture for museums. It applied to the city's Un-monument, Re-monument, De-monument initiative, which works with artists to rethink who Boston memorializes and why, after city officials reached out, WBUR reported.

SmokeSygnals convened a design group of tribal council members, historic preservation officers and cultural and education leaders. Its creative director, Steven Peters, a citizen of the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe, described the process as communal and the monument as a space for healing.
> "We don't want this to be the first and last." — Steven Peters, SmokeSygnals
Peters said the process can be replicated so that the gathering place is not the only one of its kind in the city.
Amira Madison, a member of the tribal council of the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah) who took part in the design workshops, told WBUR she hopes visitors come away with a history lesson.
## A Fraught History

Erin Genia, the city's first Indigenous Public Art and Cultural Spaces consultant in the Office of Arts and Culture and an enrolled citizen of the Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate, said there is a need for permanent representation of Indigenous peoples in Boston. She called the project an important step forward for the city's relationship with Native people.
WBUR noted that relationship has long been fraught, pointing to Massachusetts' repeal in 2005 of a colonial-era law that had barred Native Americans from Boston.
## What It Will Take

The project still needs to raise roughly $2 million and win city approvals, including from the Boston Art Commission, WBUR reported. SmokeSygnals is also exploring a cultural respect agreement that would let Indigenous groups use the land for ceremonies and gatherings with fewer bureaucratic hurdles.
The group planned to present the final design to the public at Franklin Park in October. Peters said he hopes the gathering place can be built within about two years.

sources.title: First Indigenous monument in Boston planned for Franklin Park

title: Dorchester Man, 20, Charged With Murder a Day After Fatal Shooting on Whitfield Street
dek: Joseph Bailey, 20, pleaded not guilty and was held without bail after police charged him with murder in a Sept. 30 shooting near 7 Whitfield Street in Dorchester.
body: The call came in at about 5:39 p.m. on Wednesday, Sept. 30: a person shot near 7 Whitfield Street in Dorchester. Within roughly a day, Boston police had a name and a murder charge.

Joseph Bailey, 20, of Dorchester, was arraigned Thursday, Oct. 1, in Dorchester District Court on a charge of murder, according to Boston.com, which cited court records. He pleaded not guilty and was ordered held without bail.
## The Shooting

Officers from District B-2, the Roxbury district, responded to the radio call and found a man suffering from what appeared to be a gunshot wound, the Boston Police Department said in a news release. He was taken to a local hospital, where he was later pronounced dead.
Police have not publicly identified the man. As of Thursday evening, authorities had not released his name, Boston.com reported.

Although the shooting happened in Dorchester, the first officers on scene came from District B-2, the district that covers Roxbury and Mission Hill, according to the department's account. Police have released no details about the man's age or where he lived.
## The Arrest

In its release, the department said detectives identified Bailey as a suspect after an investigation. Police did not say where or how he was taken into custody, whether a weapon was recovered, or what may have led to the shooting. No motive has been made public.
The department's release did not include any comment from officials, and Boston.com reported that information about Bailey's attorney was not immediately available.
## What Comes Next

Bailey is due back in court on Oct. 22 for a probable cause hearing, according to Boston.com. In Massachusetts, murder cases that begin in district court typically move to superior court after a grand jury indictment.

A probable cause hearing is the point at which a judge decides whether there is enough evidence for a case to move forward, though prosecutors frequently seek a grand jury indictment before that date arrives.

Police said the Homicide Unit is still investigating. Anyone with information is asked to call homicide detectives at 617-343-4470. Tips can be left anonymously with CrimeStoppers at 1-800-494-TIPS or by texting the word TIP to CRIME (27463).
The city's Neighborhood Trauma Team offers free, confidential support around the clock to people affected by violence at 617-431-0125, the department said.
Bailey is presumed innocent unless and until he is proven guilty in court.
